sentences.text: The genus name Elopteryx comes from Ancient Greek words meaning 'marsh' and 'wing'.
Charles William Andrews named the type species Elopteryx nopcsai in 1913, originally believing it to be a pelecaniform seabird.
Kálmán Lambrecht established the family Elopterygidae in 1933.

In 1975, Harrison and Walker removed several specimens from Elopteryx and redescribed them as Bradycneme draculae and Heptasteornis andrewsi, forming the family Bradycnemidae as gigantic two-meter-tall owls.
By 1978, Pierce Brodkorb became the first modern scholar to suggest the bones attributed to Elopteryx belonged to non-avian dinosaurs rather than birds.
In 1981, Dan Grigorescu and Eugen Kessler proposed that Elopteryx was a non-avian coelurosaurian dinosaur.
A 2024 study attributed a new femur specimen from Romania to Elopteryx, indicating it was secondarily flightless.
Since the 21st century, most studies have classified Elopteryx as a member of the Maniraptora and Paraves.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Elopteryx as Alvarezsauridae.
In 2024, Stoicescu and colleagues suggested that Elopteryx is a paravian member of Avialae and that Balaur bondoc is likely a junior synonym.
Elopteryx fossils were found in Late Cretaceous rocks of Romania, specifically in the Sânpetru Formation of the Hațeg Island.
The time range for Elopteryx is the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
In 2013, Stephen L. Brusatte and colleagues suggested the possibility that Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc are the same taxon, though they did not consider it the most likely scenario.

In 2019, studies debated Elopteryx's classification, with some recovering it as a basal avialan confuciusornithiform and others suggesting it forms a clade with Gargantuavis and Balaur native to the Late Cretaceous European archipelago.
Researchers have claimed that the synonymy between Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc remains possible and requires further confirmation.
